exhibitors.name: Bedrock Environmental
exhibitors.description: Erosion and sediment control, seed mixes, geotextiles, and drainage products distributed for construction, energy, and road projects
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: An erosion-control seed and supply distributor selling to contractors — distributors are filed as suppliers, and the row's identity doubt is not enough to reject the record outright.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
I tried to break this three ways and it holds.

(a) Vendor-vs-supplier: not close. offering="distributor", desc="Erosion control seed and supply", buyer="Contractors". That is squarely the DLT/Kurita pattern — a distributor of physical goods whose buyers are contractors, with municipalities at most specifying. No product, platform, or software anywhere in the row, so "vendor" would be the exact error this project has been burned by. Supplier is right.

(b) Sector/category: the run is "stormcon" (stormwater), and erosion-control seed is a stormwater/sediment-control input on construction and right-of-way work. Public Works is the closest public function and Suppliers & Services is the only category a distributor belongs in. The one alternative worth naming is Parks & Rec > Grounds, Irrigation & Turf (seed is turf), but that category is for turf-management products serving parks departments and nothing in the row points at parks buyers. For a supplier record the sector choice only decides which Suppliers & Services shelf it sits on, so the downside is small either way.

(c) The identity doubt — the strongest attack, and it still does not move the call. The flag says the site never uses "Seed & Supply" and a separate Bedrock Environmental Services, Inc. exists, so the website may be attached to the wrong entity. Run the branch both ways: if the row is the seed distributor, it is a supplier; if bedrockenvironmental.com is actually the environmental-services/consulting firm, consultancies are filed as suppliers too. Either entity lands on supplier, and neither is a govtech product company. The ambiguity is a data-hygiene problem (the website field should be re-verified before the record is promoted or contacted), not a placement problem. It is also not grounds for not_a_company — nothing suggests an agency, nonprofit, or brand line.

What I would not do on this row is treat it as a rejection or assert a public buyer: sells="unclear" and "No stated public buyer" are honest, and unclear is a real answer, not a "no". Filing it as a visible, promotable supplier is the correct handling of that state.

One caveat to carry forward rather than bury: provider="not found" and roles=null, so there is no board to wire here regardless — this is a filed record, not a live-jobs source.

exhibitors.name: Best Management Products, Inc.
exhibitors.description: Catch basin hoods and trash screens (SNOUT) that trap oil, debris and trash in storm drains, for municipal MS4s and site owners
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: It manufactures physical stormwater hardware (SNOUT hoods, stainless trash screens) that cities buy as product, not a govtech software or platform company, so it files as a supplier rather than a board vendor.

exhibitors.name: BioBase
exhibitors.description: Automated sonar mapping of lakes and ponds: bathymetry, aquatic vegetation and fish layers for water and fisheries managers
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: It is a cloud SaaS product that turns sonar logs into bathymetry and vegetation maps for waterbody owners, and universities are named among its buyers, so it is a software vendor rather than a hardware supplier.
exhibitors.verifier_why: The outcome survives, the placement does not. On the SaaS question the other researcher is right and I cannot refute it: the row says "software/SaaS" and "automated cloud processing" — BioBase is the software layer over someone else's sonar hardware (the consumer sonar logs are Lowrance/Navico's), so it is not a manufacturer, distributor, reseller, contractor or consultancy and the DLT/Kurita/Allied Universal precedent does not reach it. Parks & Rec > Park Assets is the weak link. Nothing in the row names a parks department, a municipality, or any park at all. The category is a park asset inventory; the product maps lake bottoms and aquatic vegetation. The reason given for the placement ("universities are named among its buyers") does not lead to Parks & Rec either — a campus buyer points at a limnology or grounds program, not at a city parks asset registry, and using the one public buyer in the row to justify a sector that buyer does not sit in is exactly failure mode (b). The subject matter the row actually describes — bathymetry, vegetation, and a stormwater detention-pond use case — is waterbody and water-resources management, so Public Works > Water is the defensible home if it is placed as a product row at all. Two cautions on the vendor call, both of which hold my confidence low. First, three of the four named buyers (lake associations, HOAs, golf courses) are private and "sells" is recorded as unclear, so the public-sector sale is carried entirely by the bare word "universities"; universities are genuinely public and do not disqualify, but one unelaborated noun is thin. If the gate wants a named government buyer before a company gets a real sector row, the correct fallback is Public Works > Suppliers & Services — filed, visible, promotable — not a Parks & Rec product row. Second, a brand-vs-employer risk the row does not resolve: BioBase ran for years as a Navico/Brunswick product line, and the row offers no evidence it is now an employer — provider "not found", roles null, flags say no job board. The 2024 spinout is asserted, not demonstrated. Do not promote it to a company record on the strength of the spinout line alone if the project can check it. Separately, whatever the outcome: wire_board=false. There is no board to wire, and if one is ever located under Navico or Brunswick it is a parent's board — reporting parent requisitions as BioBase's is the Rave/Motorola and RoadBotics/Michelin false positive this project has already been burned by.

exhibitors.name: Ecopliant Environmental, Inc.
exhibitors.description: Nonprofit certification body: CISEC sediment and erosion control inspector and CDSEC design certifications, exams and training
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: The row flags it as a nonprofit certification body - an inspector credentialing organization rather than an employer selling a product or service into government - so it should not become a company record.
exhibitors.verifier_why: The call leans on the "NONPROFIT" flag alone, and that is the wrong branch of the rules for this entity type. The project's supplier definition explicitly enumerates "course providers" and "trade bodies" as things that get FILED as suppliers, and the cited precedent says the same about consultancies and course providers. An erosion-and-sediment-control inspector certification body (CISEC) is exactly that: it sells certification exams, renewals and training to inspectors, contractors and agency staff. The row has sells=yes and a named public buyer ("Government agencies and municipal staff"), so it is a selling organization - not a government agency, not a brand or product line, and not a pure membership association with nothing to sell. Tax status by itself does not make a training/credentialing seller a non-company; most trade bodies the project already files as suppliers are nonprofits too, and "supplier is not a rejection" is the whole point of that bucket. It is plainly NOT a vendor - there is no govtech product or platform here, only certification and courses - so it must never get a real sector/category on the board. The sector/category chosen is fine for a supplier filing (erosion/stormwater control is Public Works; Suppliers & Services is the right bucket), which is itself a tell that the record was muddled: a not_a_company record never becomes a company record, so giving it a sector and category is self-contradictory. Two cautions from the row itself, not invented: provider="not found" and roles=null with the site last updated 2019-10, so there is no ATS to wire (wire_board=false) and the entity may be dormant or mid-rename - file it as a supplier and point it at no job board. Confidence medium: supplier-vs-not_a_company is the only live question, and the project's own precedent on course providers and trade bodies resolves it toward supplier.

exhibitors.name: Gator Guard
exhibitors.description: Sediment control wattles, weighted gutter wattles, and foam logs for construction-site and roadway erosion control
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: A wattle and foam-log manufacturer selling through a dealer and installer network to erosion-control contractors; the supplier shape is clear but the row names no public buyer at all, so its SLED relevance is unestablished rather than disproven.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
Tried to break this three ways; it holds.

(a) Vendor upgrade? No. The row describes physical goods — sediment control wattles, weighted gutter wattles, foam logs — moved through a "Dealers and Installers" page. That is a manufacturer with a two-step channel, the exact shape the project already files as supplier (Kurita hardware, DLT reseller). No product, platform, software or subscription surface appears anywhere in the row. The stated buyer is construction/erosion-control contractors, with public agencies at most specifying via highway and roadway work — the precedent line "municipalities only as specifiers" is directly on point.

(b) Wrong sector/category? Public Works > Suppliers & Services is the right home. Sediment and erosion control is stormwater and streets work; the row's own hooks are "highway, residential and industrial site development" and "IDEAL FOR ROADWAY WORK." Competing homes are weaker: Transit & Parking is riders, fare and curb systems, not roadway runoff control; Utilities & Energy is grid, billing and broadband. Water and Streets both sit under Public Works, so the sector is right either way, and Suppliers & Services is the mandated category for a supplier.

(c) Should it be not_a_company? This is the only live challenge, and it does not clear the bar. The flags — no About page, no address, no news, facts sourced from BBB — are consistent with a brand page for a product line rather than an employer, and "Gator Guard" reads like a product name. But a BBB business record is evidence of a distinct entity, parent is null, and nothing in the row identifies an owning manufacturer, so calling it a brand would be inventing the fact that not_a_company requires. Filing as a supplier is the correct, reversible call. Flag for the wiring step: if a job board is ever found on this domain, check it for parent or sibling ownership first, given how thin the site is.

One caveat on the other researcher's phrasing, not the outcome: they treat the absence of a named public buyer as leaving SLED relevance "unestablished." Under the project's rules that is simply the "unclear" state, not a mark against the record — suppliers are filed, not rejected — so it changes nothing about the placement. Confidence: medium-high on supplier and on Public Works; the residual doubt is entity-vs-brand, not shape.

exhibitors.name: Hyfi
exhibitors.description: Wireless water level sensors, flood alerts, and dashboards for municipal stormwater and flood response teams
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: Low-cost flood and sewer level sensors paired with a real-time dashboard is a monitoring product sold to city water and sewer operations - a govtech product company, not a parts supplier.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
I tried to break this on the supplier precedent and it holds. The supplier pattern in this project is a maker of parts/equipment whose real customers are contractors, engineers and distributors with municipalities only specifying (Kurita's water-treatment hardware, pipe and precast, DLT reselling, Allied's guards). Hyfi does not match that shape: the row names cities as the buyer directly — Chicago (with Verizon and CNT) and New Orleans — not a distributor channel, and the offering is sensors paired with a real-time dashboard, i.e. a deployed monitoring product with a software layer that a water/sewer department logs into, which is what makes it a govtech product company rather than a parts vendor. "Monitoring hardware/sensors" alone was the one thing that could have flipped it, but hardware plus a city-facing dashboard sold to city operations is the same shape as other IoT monitoring platforms on the board, not a catalog part.

Placement also survives: flood and sewer level monitoring is municipal stormwater/wastewater work, and Public Works > Water is the only category that fits. I considered Public Safety > Emergency Mgmt because of "flood," but the run context is stormcon and the sensors sit in the sewer/stormwater system serving water operations, not an EOC alerting product; Utilities & Energy has no water category at all, so it is not an alternative.

Two cautions that do not change the outcome but should ride with the record. First, wire_board must be false: the row says "no job board," provider "not found," roles null — with 8 employees there is nothing to wire, and the named partners (Verizon, CNT) and the University of Michigan are a parent/partner trap, so under no circumstances should a Verizon or U-M requisition feed be attached to Hyfi. Second, at 8 employees and $1M raised this is a vendor record with essentially no sales hiring to surface; it belongs on the board as a company but will stay empty until it grows. Neither is a reason to downgrade the outcome — a vendor with no openings is still a vendor.

exhibitors.name: Precip
exhibitors.description: Hyperlocal rainfall measurement and forecast app and API: rain alerts, multi-site rainfall history, and data export for field teams
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: The row does not support a vendor call: the identity match is unconfirmed and the site names no stormwater use and no public buyer, so it is filed rather than boarded and should be held for verification.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
The reasoning refutes itself. It says "the row does not support a vendor call: the identity match is unconfirmed and the site names no stormwater use and no public buyer" — and then makes a positive placement anyway. Supplier is not a low-confidence parking space; it is a substantive business-model finding (pipe and precast, distributors, resellers, contractors, consultancies, course providers, guards — DLT, Kurita, Allied Universal). Nothing in this row puts Precip in that class. The row says offering="software/SaaS" and desc="Rainfall data app": a three-person YC software product is the opposite of the supplier archetype. On the row's own facts the only two defensible readings are (1) a govtech data product, which would be a VENDOR, or (2) a consumer/ag/insurance weather-data startup with no public buyer at all — and the row cannot distinguish them, so neither call can be made.

The sector is worse than the outcome. "Public Works" rests on one thing: the run label "stormcon". The row's own evidence cuts against it — why="Site never mentions stormwater", sells="unclear", buyer="Unknown". Filing it under Public Works asserts a stormwater/water application the row explicitly says the site never claims. That is exactly failure mode (b): a sector the actual product is not shown to serve, inherited from the source list rather than from the company.

And the identity is not established. The flags say plainly: "UNCERTAIN MATCH: only match found is precip.ai, a three-person YC rainfall-data app; getprecip.com failed robots.txt. UNCONFIRMED." The StormCon exhibitor may well be getprecip.com — a different entity that was never read. Filing under the unverified URL creates a company record for a possibly wrong company, with a website, a sector and a category attached to it. A supplier record is not harmless: the project keeps ~4,745 of them visible and promotable, so a misattributed one is a live wrong record, not a quiet archive.

If verification later shows precip.ai is the exhibitor and it sells rainfall/precipitation data to municipal stormwater or utility departments, the correct call is vendor, Public Works > Water — a data platform sold to a public works department is a product company, not a supplier, so "Suppliers & Services" would be wrong in that case too. If it turns out to be the consumer/ag rainfall app the description suggests, with no public buyer named, it does not belong on the board in any bucket. Either way the current row supports neither call, and "unclear" is the honest answer until someone reaches getprecip.com and confirms which Precip exhibited and who buys it.

Separately, there is nothing lost by holding it: provider="not found" and roles=null, so there is no job board to wire, and at three people there would be no SLED sales openings for a salesperson to see even if the match were confirmed.

exhibitors.name: REHAU
exhibitors.description: Polymer building products: PEXa plumbing and radiant piping, MUNICIPEX water service lines, and RAUSIKKO stormwater storage crates
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: A global polymer piping and building-products maker whose named customers are contractors and distributors, so at best it is a supplier, and the row names no public buyer at all.
exhibitors.verifier_why: I tried to break this three ways and it holds. (1) Outcome: REHAU is a polymer extrusion manufacturer (pipe, window/building profiles, furniture and industrial polymers) whose row-stated buyers are "Contractors and distributors," with no public buyer named anywhere in the row. That is exactly the project's own precedent pattern — a Kurita-style hardware maker, with municipalities at most specifying the pipe. It is not a govtech product or platform company, so "vendor" is not defensible; "not_a_company" is also wrong, because REHAU is a real employer with its own careers system, not a brand or product line. Supplier is the correct file, and filing it keeps it visible and promotable. (2) Sector: the offering is "manufactured products (pipe, structures, treatment devices)" from a stormwater run — municipal stormwater/sewer/water infrastructure. Public Works owns Water, so Public Works is the right home. The plausible alternative, Utilities & Energy, covers grid, broadband and billing, not buried stormwater pipe, so it would be a worse fit; Housing & Community Dev would only apply if we were filing the window-profile/building-products line, which is not what this row describes. (3) Category: Suppliers & Services is the only correct category for a supplier outcome. Two cautions that do not change the placement but should ride with the record: the ATS (ukg/UltiPro) sits under parent "REHAU Group," so wiring it risks reporting parent/sibling requisitions as this company's — treat wire_board as false unless the instance is proven scoped to the US entity; and a global polymer group's UKG instance will be dominated by plant, extrusion and automotive roles rather than SLED sales, which is board-noise risk on top of the parent problem.

exhibitors.name: Santa Fe Water Systems

exhibitors.is_govtech_why: Sells water and wastewater equipment to municipal utilities, which is equipment supply into the public sector rather than a govtech product.

exhibitors.name: SEKISUI CHEMICAL CO., LTD.

exhibitors.is_govtech_why: A Japanese chemicals and plastics conglomerate whose business is mostly electronics, automotive, housing and medical, with pipe systems and pipeline renewal as one segment - a materials manufacturer, not a govtech vendor.

exhibitors.name: Silt Tracker
exhibitors.description: SWPPP inspection and maintenance-tracking app for construction-site sediment and erosion control compliance
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: A stormwater inspection and SWPPP compliance SaaS product with municipalities named as buyers - a genuine govtech software vendor, placed under Public Works: Water because stormwater compliance is its subject.
exhibitors.verifier_why: I tried to break this one three ways and it held. (a) Supplier test: the supplier bucket in this project catches manufacturers, distributors, resellers, field contractors, consultancies, guards and course providers — Silt Tracker is none of those. The row says offering="software/SaaS" and desc="Stormwater inspection and SWPPP compliance software", i.e. it is the product, not a firm that performs inspections or sells erosion-control goods. It is not a Kurita/DLT/Allied Universal analogue. (b) Buyer test: "Contractors and municipalities for SWPPP compliance" does name a public buyer directly, so it is not an "unclear". The strongest adversarial point is that contractors are named FIRST and construction-site SWPPP inspection under an NPDES construction permit is largely a contractor workflow — so this could be construction-tech with municipalities incidental. But a mixed contractor/municipal buyer base does not demote a software product to supplier under this project's rules; MS4/municipal stormwater programs are a real named buyer here, and the correct treatment of a partly-public SaaS is vendor, not supplier. (c) Placement test: stormwater/drainage compliance is a public works function (stormwater utility / MS4 program sits under Public Works in essentially every US municipality), and Public Works: Water is the only category in the taxonomy whose subject is water. Nothing in Utilities & Energy, General Gov or Housing & Community Dev fits better. Two caveats that do not change the verdict: provider="not found" and roles=null, so there is no ATS evidence in this row — wire_board cannot be set true on this evidence, and the record would be a board entry with no live requisitions until a provider is found. And the row gives no headcount or corporate-structure signal at all (parent=null is an absence of evidence, not proof of independence); if a later pass shows Silt Tracker is a product line of an erosion-control services firm rather than a standalone employer, this flips to not_a_company. On the row as given, vendor / Public Works / Water is the right call.

exhibitors.name: Sioux Chief Manufacturing Co., Inc.
exhibitors.description: Plumbing products for wholesalers and contractors: drains, trench drains, PEX, valves, hangers, and outlet boxes
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: A plumbing products manufacturer selling through wholesalers and contractors with no public buyer named anywhere in the row - the weakest supplier in this batch, filed rather than rejected because it is still a real employer, not an agency or a brand.
exhibitors.verifier_why: I tried to break this three ways and it holds. (1) Not a vendor: Sioux Chief is a rough-plumbing products manufacturer — pipe fittings, drains, carriers, water-hammer arrestors — sold through wholesalers and contractors. The row's own offering field says "manufactured products (pipe, structures, treatment devices)" and buyer says "Plumbing wholesalers and contractors." That is the project's precedent case almost verbatim: a manufacturer whose buyers are contractors, engineers and distributors, with municipalities only as specifiers, is a supplier (same shelf as Kurita's water-treatment hardware and the pipe/precast makers). There is no product, platform, software, or subscription in the row, so "vendor" is not available. (2) Not not_a_company: it is a real, privately held employer with its own Paylocity ATS and no parent listed, so there is no parent-board trap and no brand/agency/nonprofit problem — filing beats rejecting. (3) Sector: this is the only place I had real doubt. Sioux Chief's line is building-side plumbing, not municipal mains or stormwater treatment, so an argument exists for a buildings/facilities home rather than Public Works. But among the valid sectors there is no buildings/facilities option, the row was harvested on the stormcon (stormwater) run, and pipe/drainage/treatment hardware sits closest to Public Works > Water. Public Works > Suppliers & Services is therefore the correct catch-all — Utilities & Energy would be worse (that is grid, lighting, billing, broadband) and General Gov worse still. The reason text is also honest about the weakness rather than inventing a public buyer, which is the right call given the row names none. Note for the record, not a defect in the placement: nothing in this row supports wiring the board — no roles count, and no evidence of SLED sales postings — so this should stay a filed supplier record and not be pointed at a job feed on this evidence.

exhibitors.name: Soleno
exhibitors.description: HDPE pipe, culverts, geocellular retention, and stormwater treatment units for infrastructure, agricultural, and residential drainage
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: Makes thermoplastic drainage pipe and stormwater management products for municipalities and contractors - a pipe manufacturer, which this project files as a supplier by precedent.

exhibitors.name: Stalker Radar (Applied Concepts, Inc.)
exhibitors.description: Police radar and lidar, photo enforcement cameras, and radar speed signs for law enforcement and traffic agencies
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: Sells speed radar, lidar and radar speed signs directly to law enforcement agencies, cities and schools on cooperative contracts - the agency is the buyer, not a specifier, so this is a public safety vendor despite arriving on a stormwater exhibitor list.
exhibitors.verifier_why: Sector is right (police speed enforcement, not stormwater), but the outcome rests on a test the project does not use. The researcher's reason is "the agency is the buyer, not a specifier, so this is a public safety vendor." Buying direct from the agency is not what makes a vendor: Allied Universal sells guards straight to public agencies and Kurita sells water-treatment hardware to utilities, and both are filed as SUPPLIERS in this project's own precedent. Direct agency purchase only rules OUT the specifier-only pattern; it does not rule IN a govtech product company. The vendor test is whether this is a govtech PRODUCT or PLATFORM company, and on this row it is not. The row's own offering field says "manufactured products," and the desc is "police speed radar, lidar, speed trailers and radar speed signs" - hardware instruments, exactly the rubric's explicit supplier bucket ("equipment manufacturers"). Nothing in the row names software, a platform, a hosted data service, a subscription or an agency-facing application; the only sales-motion evidence is cooperative contracts (HGACBuy, NY OGS), which is how commodity public-safety equipment (firearms, uniforms, vehicle upfits) is bought and is therefore neutral-to-negative evidence for "product company." Reaching "vendor" requires inventing a software line, which is forbidden. Correct filing is Public Safety > Suppliers & Services - a filing, not a rejection; it stays visible and promotable. Two secondary notes: (1) "Stalker Radar" is a brand of Applied Concepts, Inc. and the parent field repeats that same legal entity, so the prevue board is the employer's own, not a parent's or sibling's - no Rave/Motorola trap here, wire_board is fine on that ground; (2) roles is null, so the row shows no actual SLED sales opening, and confidence in anything beyond the supplier filing should be low.

exhibitors.name: Storm Water Systems
exhibitors.description: Floating litter traps and trash booms (Bandalong, StormX) for city and county waterways, with installation and consulting services
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: The closest call in this batch: it sells direct to city and county stormwater programs and adds installation and consulting, but Bandalong and StormX are physical litter traps and booms, which is water-infrastructure hardware in the same class as Kurita's water-treatment equipment rather than a govtech product or platform.

exhibitors.name: StormTek (product of SWIMS, an Apex company)
exhibitors.description: Stainless connector pipe screens for California full trash capture compliance, sold by SWIMS with storm drain maintenance services
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: StormTek is a product of SWIMS (itself acquired by Apex Companies), so the row names a brand, not an employer - and the only buyers named are private property managers and HOA boards.
exhibitors.verifier_why: The brand/not-a-company call is aimed at the wrong half of the row. "StormTek" is indeed a product line, but the row's website is swimsclean.com - SWIMS's own site - and the row name already carries the operating company. SWIMS is a real employer: a Northern/Southern California field maintenance contractor doing storm drain, catch basin and vault cleaning, with 3 roles posted on its OWN careers page (provider: "own page, no ATS detected"), so the requisitions belong to the operating company, not to a brand and not to a parent board. not_a_company is reserved for agencies, nonprofits/associations, and brands with no employer behind them; here the employer is right there and the defect is a naming defect. The fix is to rename the record to SWIMS (StormTek) and file it, not to delete it. On the project's own precedent - field contractors, maintenance crews, consultancies filed as suppliers, never rejected - SWIMS is a textbook Public Works / Suppliers & Services entry: storm drain, catch basin and vault maintenance is public-works infrastructure work even where the named buyers are private. It is emphatically not a vendor (no govtech product or platform; manufactured pipe/structures/treatment devices plus a cleaning service), so the reviewer's sector/category is the right destination - they just attached it to an outcome that throws the record away. Two secondary problems: (1) assigning a sector and category to a not_a_company outcome is internally contradictory, since such records are never supposed to become company records; (2) the private-buyer argument ("property managers and HOA boards") is a weak basis for rejection under the project's own rule that a row naming no public buyer is "unclear," never "no" - sells is literally recorded as "unclear," and the reason statement leans on it as if it were a proven negative. Separately, wire_board should be FALSE regardless of outcome: SWIMS was acquired by Apex Companies in May 2024, so hiring is likely to route to Apex's board, and reporting a parent's requisitions as the subsidiary's is the exact Rave/Motorola and RoadBotics/Michelin failure this project has been burned by; the 3 roles on a non-ATS page show no evidence of a SLED sales seat. Confidence: medium - judging only from the row, which names no public-agency buyer, so this sits at the boundary if the project applies a hard public-buyer test. But the choice between supplier and not_a_company is not close: an employer with its own careers page is not a brand.
